reasons: The lake identity record names Hill v. California, U.S. Supreme Court, decided 1971-04-05, year 1971.
The lake citation fields match the asserted official citation, parallel citations, and vendor-neutral citation.
The opinion directly addresses whether a valid mistaken-identity arrest can support a search incident to arrest.
The role is limited to Related (cross-doctrine), which fits because the case is not just a pure SIA-person-search case but does decide a search-incident consequence.
residual_risks: No separate SIA Persons home-page definition was disclosed; this review verifies only the relationship from the disclosed Hill materials.

defect.evidence_quote: permissible in scope under pre-Chimel standards
defect.problem: The arrest rule is supported, but the search-incident clause is too broad unless it is limited to the scope otherwise permitted by search-incident doctrine; Hill upheld the apartment search under pre-Chimel standards because Chimel was not retroactive.
defect.proposed_fix: An arrest of the wrong person is valid where police have probable cause to arrest one person and reasonably, in good faith, mistake the arrestee for that person; a search incident to that arrest is valid only to the extent the law would have allowed the search had the arrestee actually been the suspect, and Hill upheld the apartment search under pre-Chimel standards.

reasons: The opinion supports the mistaken-identity arrest rule and says the officers' mistake was understandable and reasonable.
The opinion also states police could do what the law would have allowed if Miller had been Hill, so the SIA portion needs that limiting condition.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add the pre-Chimel/otherwise-lawful-scope limitation to the short holding.

reasons: Hill turns on probable cause to arrest Hill plus a reasonable mistaken identification of Miller.
The opinion invokes practical probable-cause reasonableness and cites Brinegar, so placement as Probable Cause progeny is supported.
residual_risks: No separate Probable Cause home-page taxonomy was disclosed; this review verifies doctrinal fit from the Hill record.
